claims.text: On-the-fly active learning during phase-transition simulations can substantially reduce computational cost while retaining near-DFT fidelity.
The proposed method can be applied to elemental or binary systems near their fusion points.
The intended benchmark systems have well-characterized ab initio free-energy landscapes for both solid and fluid states.
An active-learning MLP can selectively trigger DFT calculations when it encounters configurations with high predictive uncertainty.
Near melting, vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron-vibration coupling are critical to the thermodynamic calculation.
Active learning automatically generates training data tailored to the relevant configuration space while requiring relatively few DFT calculations.
Updating the MLP from local configurations encountered during high-uncertainty events balances computational cost against free-energy and entropy accuracy.
Restricting new DFT evaluations to high-error regions of configuration space minimizes unnecessary ab initio calculations.
The active-learning method will produce accurate solid and liquid free-energy surfaces.
The active-learning method will faithfully retain the entropy contributions needed for fusion thermodynamics.
The method will achieve approximately an order-of-magnitude cost reduction relative to full AIMD.
The method will achieve approximately an order-of-magnitude cost reduction relative to TOR-TILD.
Predicted free energies, melting points, and latent heats will agree with full AIMD within about 5%.
Standard AIMD and TOR-TILD continuously compute free energies without adaptive model updates.
The method should perform best for elemental or binary systems having moderate configurational complexity near their fusion temperatures.
Extension to multicomponent high-entropy systems may be more difficult because their phase spaces are more complex.
Extreme anharmonicity or complex electronic interactions may reduce the attainable cost savings or fidelity.
Failure to agree with AIMD by 5% or better, or failure to reduce cost by at least tenfold, is proposed as the decisive falsification criterion.
